around.headline: Fake 'CM' WhatsApp video call cons Bengaluru man out of Rs 1 lakh with promise of Rs 11 lakh aid
around.summary: A scammer posing as "CM Vijay" over a WhatsApp video call promised a Bengaluru man Rs 11 lakh in government aid, then got him to pay Rs 1 lakh as an upfront fee, per TOI. No genuine government scheme ever asks you to pay a fee to release money you're owed.

around.headline: Man arrested for taking obscene photos of Bengaluru woman, then blackmailing her
around.summary: Police arrested a man accused of secretly photographing a woman and threatening to circulate the images unless she complied with his demands, per NDTV. If you're targeted this way, report it to the cyber crime cell rather than paying or complying — threatening to share such images is a criminal offence regardless of how they were obtained.

around.headline: Fake cancer drugs sold to 90+ Bengaluru hospitals; pharmacy owner arrested
around.summary: Police arrested a pharmacy owner and seized a large stock of counterfeit medicines supplied to more than 90 hospitals across the city, per The Indian Express and The Hindu. If a family member is on cancer treatment, ask the hospital to confirm the batch and manufacturer of any drug sourced through a third-party pharmacy.

around.headline: 529 child labourers rescued in citywide crackdown; 105 cases registered
around.summary: A large joint rescue operation across Bengaluru freed 529 child labourers from workplaces including markets and small units, with 105 cases registered against employers, per The Hindu and TOI. You can report suspected child labour anonymously to Childline on 1098.

around.headline: Partial Pink Line opening won't ease Bannerghatta Road traffic, say commuters
around.summary: Experts and commuters say the partial opening of the Pink Line metro corridor won't meaningfully cut congestion on Bannerghatta Road, while private cab and auto operators are separately threatening to protest a new digital-meter mandate, per The Hindu and Deccan Herald. Don't expect quick relief on Bannerghatta Road, and watch for possible auto/cab availability disruptions if the protest goes ahead.

around.headline: Bengaluru tenant got back just ₹19,000 of a ₹1.3 lakh deposit — what the law actually says
around.summary: A Bengaluru tenant received only a fraction of their security deposit after arbitrary deductions by the landlord, prompting a look at what rental law actually allows, per Livemint. Photograph the flat's condition at move-in and move-out — landlords can't legally deduct for normal wear and tear.

around.headline: Oil prices jump 3% after Saudi pipeline attack; Asian markets slide
around.summary: Crude oil prices rose roughly 3% after an attack on a Saudi pipeline, and Asian stock markets slid on the news alongside fears of an AI-sector slowdown, per The Indian Express and Investing.com. A sustained rise in oil prices typically shows up at Indian petrol pumps within a few weeks.

events.note: Ulsoor Lake has been readied to receive the immersion of roughly 1 lakh Ganesha idols as the festival's visarjan days continue, per TOI.

events.note: Temples across the city are seeing large crowds as immersion processions continue; Bengaluru Police have stepped up security along procession routes, per Udayavani and ThePrint.

street_smart.title: You get a WhatsApp video call from a man in what looks like a government office, introducing himself as 'CM Vijay' and saying you're eligible for ₹11 lakh under a special relief scheme — exactly the call that conned a Bengaluru man out of Rs 1 lakh today. He says the funds are ready to transfer to your account right now, but a one-time 'processing and verification fee' needs to go through first. What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: TOI Bengaluru, Sept 13-14 — a Bengaluru man lost Rs 1 lakh after a scammer impersonating 'CM Vijay' promised him Rs 11 lakh in government aid over a WhatsApp video call. This fake-government-aid-disbursement scam mechanism hasn't been used as a street-smart scenario in the last three weeks.
street_smart.situation: The caller has government-looking documents visible behind him on screen, already knows your full name and address, and is pressuring you to pay within the next 10 minutes before the 'scheme window closes'.

choices.text: Hang up without paying anything, and independently verify by calling your ward office or checking the scheme's name on the official Karnataka government portal you look up yourself — never through any link or number the caller gives you.
choices.feedback: Correct. No genuine government scheme ever asks you to pay a fee to receive money you're owed. Verify only through official channels you find yourself, and report the number to the national cyber crime helpline 1930.

choices.text: Pay the 'processing fee' via UPI since the caller already knows your personal details and the scheme sounds legitimate, then wait for the ₹11 lakh to arrive.
choices.feedback: This is the trap. Scammers routinely have your name and address from data leaks or public records — none of that verifies the call, and once you pay the 'fee' there is no ₹11 lakh coming, only further requests.

choices.text: Ask the caller to send the scheme details on WhatsApp first, and only pay if the document looks official with a government emblem.
choices.feedback: Risky. A convincing PDF with a government emblem and letterhead is trivial to fake with basic design tools — it isn't proof of anything.

choices.text: Refuse to pay but stay on the call to draw out more details so you can report the scammer later.
choices.feedback: Risky. Every extra minute you stay engaged gives a scammer more chances to pressure or socially engineer you into slipping up — hang up and report; you don't need to interrogate them yourself.

takeaways: No real government scheme ever asks for a fee to release funds you're owed — that's always the tell of a scam, however official-looking the caller or documents are.
Scammers having your name, address or other personal details doesn't make a call legitimate — this data is often leaked or bought, not proof of authority.
Report suspicious calls or messages to the national cyber crime helpline 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in, and never use a number or link the caller themselves provides to 'verify'.

quiz.question: How much money did the Bengaluru man lose to the fake 'CM Vijay' WhatsApp video-call scam?
quiz.why: The scammer had promised ₹11 lakh in aid but only ever intended to collect the upfront 'fee' — a nurse and a friend separately lost Rs 29.8 lakh to an online investment scam reported the same day.

quiz.question: How many child labourers were rescued in Bengaluru's latest citywide crackdown?
quiz.why: 105 cases were registered against employers in the same operation; you can report suspected child labour anonymously to Childline on 1098.

quiz.question: Which country's pipeline was attacked, sending oil prices up roughly 3% and adding to a slide in Asian stock markets?
quiz.why: Oil-price shocks from Gulf infrastructure attacks tend to reach Indian petrol pumps within a few weeks.

quiz.question: Under Indian tenancy norms, can a landlord deduct security-deposit money for normal wear and tear on a rented flat?
options: No — only for actual damage beyond normal wear and tear
Only if it's written into the agreement
Only for flats older than 5 years
quiz.why: Normal wear and tear — faded paint, minor scuffs — is expected with everyday living and isn't legally deductible; only genuine damage is.

quiz.question: Which blood type is known as the 'universal donor', safe to give to patients of any blood type in an emergency?
quiz.why: O negative red blood cells lack the A, B and Rh antigens that trigger transfusion reactions, which is why they're kept on hand for emergencies before blood-type testing is done.
